commentBody:
Woo Davis!

(That's where I am.)

I found this to be a reasonably tough Saturday puzzle, with a bunch of toeholds and fingerholds at first. But after a bit it was possible to finish despite a number of letter formations that looked very unlikely. Like the SST at the end of the summer shirt. There were a bunch of cute deceptive clues, too. NIce!
A couple of spots strained my brain. Then it was done. Fun. Not hard.

Having been the recipient of lots of clue-bullying in the past, I’m scared of KAC puzzles.  Some of them have been way hard.  Solving this one while Mr. Collins is in a kind mood.  Nice Saturday puzzle!
I'm from Davis and went to school at UCD, so that made this easier, with some easier answers like spanakopita.  I finished in just over 21 minutes which is a decent time (for me.).

16:14 for a Saturday. Definitely a PB. And on my birthday! Sweet.

Fun puzzle, but not too challenging IMO

Looking forward to those KAC puzzles where the clue-bullying is back. Because 30A, 42A, and 9D were Monday level clues. And Mr. Collins is my favorite constructor for a SATURDAY puzzle! Still plenty of brilliance, though. Glad he understands our plight.

This was the EPITOME of a solid Saturday puzzle.  I was fortunate enough to have enough gimmes to be able to solve it in a reasonable time.  Seeing SLEEVELESST two rows above STEEVE had me a bit peeved.

Solid and mostly enjoyable Saturday save for a couple names I didn’t know (DANSKO, ALFRE). I had MENSCAPS for a while because LAYMAN didn’t come to mind, but that’s a great clue for both 36 across AND down. 

I don’t like SLEEVELESST, but I’ll get over it.
Pretty straightforward for a Saturday. The NW corner was the last to fall.
I thought "sleeveless t, no,  it can't be," but yes!  Also, I had howl versus hoot, which had me sidetracked or a while.
"Influencer" has the same letter count as STREETTEAM. Just sayin'.
Never heard of STEEVE, and had no idea what letter bond followed SERIES. But any other letter would have less likely. Found my mistake in the MINARET/SPANAKOPITA crossing (had an e).

Agree with Caitlin this is a bit of a Kameron lite—but not a gimme by any means and still fun and fresh. Loved the LENSCAP clue.

Can’t wait for the return to form of some good old Kameron bullying though—bring it on!

Before we get too many shouts of Naticks, no, I don’t think this was one. I didn’t known what letter to put after SERIES either, and hadn’t heard of SKEEVE—but  STREETT_AM could only be an E, and then STEEV_ could only be an E after that, so that seems like fair game for a Saturday especially. DAP was my other no-know and had FILE before PILE but not hard to suss that one out either.

KAC is back! 

'Tis a SOFTEr, gentler KAC, but according to his notes this was a temporary THAW and we should expect more clue-bullying in the future. And here I was, thinking I had gotten smarter or more skilled...

Very nice to see O. Henry's "The Gift of the MAGI" in the grid. I read it as a 13-year-old and thought it was the most romantic and most poignant tale I had ever read. 

Also loved the presence of EPITOME. It's such a great word, even more so since the day I learned to pronounce it correctly. Up until then, I only knew it from reading and would say epi-TOME, thinking myself oh so grown-up. 
I'd love to say that, after that, I became more careful about voicing words I only knew from reading, but no, I continued to embarrass myself. 
(These days I do check online for pronunciations.)

I had a very good time with this solve.
Thank you, KAC, for one HELLUVA puzzle!
Well below average time, yet felt difficult the whole way. A proper Saturday test.

(Emu-proofed version)

KAC is back! 

'Tis a SOFTEr, gentler KAC, but according to his notes this was a temporary THAW and we should expect more clue-bullying in the future. 
And here I was, thinking I had gotten smarter or more skilled...

Very nice to see O. Henry's "The Gift of the MAGI" in the grid. I read it as a 13-year-old and thought it was the most romantic and most poignant tale I had ever read. 

Also loved the presence of EPITOME. It's such a great word, even more so since the day I learned to pronounce it correctly! Up until then, I only knew it from reading and would say epi-TOME, thinking myself oh so grown-up. 

I'd love to say that, after that, I became more careful about voicing words I only knew from reading, but no, I continued to embarrass myself. (These days I do check online for pronunciations.) 

I had a very good time with this solve. Thank you, KAC, for one H3LLUV@  puzzle!
Steeve and stevedore share the same roots in Spanish. Phew!

What Caitlin and KAC said. But Don't Cry for Me, Argentina. A puzzle with such lovely occupants is okay by me. Looking at you, ERIC CARLE, SPANAKOPITA, COMTE cheese, Michelle, ma BELLE AMIE. Also,  tonight I learned STEEVE and PENG.

And let's not forget ALFRE Woodard. I've heard the 90s are back, so I'll put in a plug for the 1992 movie by John Sayles starring Mary McDonnell and ALFRE called Passion Fish. 

Meanwhile here she is seen briefly with Trombone Shorty in a Playing for Change video.

What does an author do with an epipen?

Writes an epitome!

Lively puzzle, love the mini French theme, what a hoot! I have learned now that the French say "Oh la la," and that in English, people say "ooh la la" 93% of the time, and "oo la la" as it is here, only 7% of the time (as of 2019, according to google ngram). But it is said. I'm surprised, given all the French, given we have rear end and ar$es that we didn't get derriere -- and I don't know how I remembered serviettes but managed to pull the word out of my own derriere.  (Excuse the French).

Whoosh! Had to go back and double-check it was KAC. But of course, the usual terrific smorgasbord of fun and quirky stuff. (I thought I was so clever dropping in viscOMETER. Hey, it made sense to me.)

One of those puzzles where I wasn’t sure about many of the answers when filling them in, but somehow I muddled my way through with a half decent time (under half an hour). Fun diversion while waiting for some banana bread to bake :)

I noticed how both Caitlin and Kameron both obliquely reference and neatly sidestep the Great Easening controversy in column and comments, respectively.

Fun A.E. Saturday.

I found this puzzle extremely hard but ultimately doable. I enjoyed the challenge.

Initially I was put off by how many entries I simply didn't know. However, I persisted, liberally using the app's pencil feature to tentatively type in some answers. With time I seemed to have tuned into the constructor's wavelength, which helped me deal with the smart ambiguity and misdirection of the clues.

I also had several epiphanies: to my surprise I realized I knew ERIC CARLE from previous puzzles (even though the caterpillar thing is unknown to me and I had no idea the guy had anything to do with it: the name I spontaneously remembered just fit with the crosses; before you find this strange, consider if you know Kornel Makuszyński and his "Koziołek Matołek") and I recalled the term EN PASSANT, even though I don't know what it means.

I owe knowing SPANAKOPITA to "Bojack Horseman" - it was the name of one of the characters. As I watched the show I though: hey, that's that Greek spinach pastry! And I've remembered it since.

RIATA was new to me. Too bad I'll probably forget it by tomorrow. Ditto HEM AND HAW.

How is a SLEEVELESS T a T? Isn't it an I? Seriously though, wouldn't that be a tank top rather than a tee?

(I'm off on holiday tomorrow so this is probably my last post in August. See you in September)

CL: you mean PACK a punch, i assume. Pulling a punch means the exact opposite.

 “Kameron Austin Collins as a sharp, witty constructor whose grids can pull a fearsome punch.”

If you’ve heard the expression “don’t pull any punches, you probably know it means “tell me the unvarnished truth — i can take it.” Good pro wrestlers are quite accomplished at making harmless blows look real. 

I’m sure I could have broken this to you more gently, but the irony would have given me indigestion. Thank you.

Wow I had a bunch of negative thoughts on this puzzle. But now I see it is KAC. One of my favorites. I’m conflicted. 

This was a very quick solve for me. and super quick for a KAC. 

Okay. My complaints. Which may or may not be valid. I’ll presume the latter. 

SLEVELESS T.  I don’t know why. But I find just the letter T to be an abomination. I know T-shirt.  But still…

OOLALA. where is the H?

I ain’t never heard of TRAGICOMIC.  but one C?

I did appreciate the new? Clue for ETNA. 

I know 97% of you sang “don’t cry for me Argentina” when filling out 26Down. 

A pretty easy late week, relatively speaking.

This was really unsatisfying for me. Like a joke that you get but it doesn't seem like it quite works and so it doesn't end up being funny.
That and a bunch of esoteric trivia.
Saturdays are really hit-or-miss for me, so I assume that some satisfied saturday lovers out there are glad for this puzzle.

Like everybody else I'm gonna call foul on SLEEVELESS T-- it should be either "sleeveless T-shirt" or "sleeveless tee"-- but otherwise I didn't mind this one, and EN PASSANT happened to remind me of the beautiful lilac perfume by Olivia Giacobetti. (It's the NYT crossword, so I get to say things like that.)
I just watched the Obama Meet & Greet sketch again. They never say that word. I kept trying to make DOG or FAM fit but I knew they wouldn’t. Ruined the puzzle for me.

If you have ever made spanakopita, that clue was a gimme before you finished reading it—one of the more challenging spinach dishes.  I can't believe how often I used to launch into complicated recipes (dolmas were a lot of fun, washing the grape leaves and stuffing them, one after a dammed endless other, ratatouille that I made by the cast iron cauldronful, moussaka—you name it, I knew it could be done if you could read (creative flourishes came later), and now I find goosing up a frozen pizza to make it worth eating to be a staggeringly arduous task.

People used to love parties, and if you invited people to a party, they always came, showing up with wine and desserts and all sorts of wonderful things.  

Online friends are lovely, but where's the food?
I learned "serviette in French class.  Never associated it with the U.K.

I finished it in 9:19 and was thinking "this was a good Wednesday puzzle", then looked up my average Wednesday solve time and found it's 11:29. (An average Saturday is 24:09.) So basically this was an easy Wednesday or a mildly challenging Tuesday (average 8:30). Ho hum, to the archives I go.

Haven't heard SERVIETTE since the 90s but perhaps it's still used down south.

Fell at DAH and BALLERS. 

I liked my solution that to waffle was a HEMANsHoW and I’m not familiar with the Obama comedy sketch. 

a fair Saturday by recent standards. I knew the campus, never heard of the shoes, nor the actress, war bonds, etc but they could all be deduced. 

I was about to write something awful about sleeveless T-shirts and decided to leave it at this comment.

I was irked by some of the clueing and some of the answers. I don’t like it when it seems forced. Like with a joke or a riddle, the clue should give way to an “aha” punchline that makes you think “Oh, that’s clever!” 

Sometimes I think “That can’t seriously be the answer, can it?”  (ARSES). 

Sometimes I think “That must be the answer but I’m not sure i get it, or it’s just very weak” (LAYMAN, ALA)

Sometimes I think “I’ve never heard of that and it seems unlikely but it has to be right” (ALFRE, DANSKO — i guess there’s a difference between a “big name” and a “household name”)

But I LOVE SPANAKOPITA, so there’s that.
Fun 👍

Tough in a good way…. A nice Saturday. I had DOG for DAP for ages as I’d not seen the sketch so was looking for a four letter word beginning with G for Crowd (in)…
 Never heard of Eric Carle or Series E either!

Sleeves off to Caitlin for finding that column photo.

What did the stevedore say after a particularly satisfying potato chip?
That was a HELLUVA LAY MAN

What a treat!!! Kameron is my absolute favorite constructor by a mile, I wish he were more of a regular contributor! 
NYT: are you listening? 
Let this guy make all your puzzles
OO LA LA! Hints of some vintage KAC in the hopper? Sign me up! SERVIETTES immediately brought this Trevor Noah bit to mind: https://youtu.be/Vcv5_3fQRNc?si=TTz5iotbru3khNfB

Kameron's lost a little something off his fastball.

On the other hand, it's good for the ego to be able to hit him once in a while.

Lots of nice French terms for gimmes helped get this one off the ground, giving me a stab at all the unknowns (shoes, actor, company etc). Remembered how to spell SPANAKOPITA, yum.
SERVIETTES, while correct, made me pause. Perhaps it’s regional, or, goddess forgive classist, but I would use that term for paper wipes only, napkin for cloth ones used for actual dining. Just me?

Couple of very obscure/archaic entries (STEEVE,RIATA) that I found a bit surprising for NYT, even on a Saturday. That said, the main issue was that I immediately got hurl for 1A, then got heat and reheat for 1D and 3D, then solved the rest of the crossword before coming back and spending ten minutes wondering why I couldn’t get answers for the NW corner. After begrudgingly accepting that SLEEVELESS T must be right, I eventually unpicked and realised I’d just gone badly wrong. Not my favourite, but then Saturdays seldom are.

Really tough one for me. A few US specific things amongst some difficult others. 

But I must protest 'lenscap'. One of the worst clues I've seen in a while. The constructor thought they were a little too clever with that one...
I love when crosses imply an impossible word (like the last three letters being SST). It's a thrill when the impossible reveals itself. This was such a good puzzle, fun, fair, and challenging.

Big shoutout to Nardwaur ("The Human Serviette") because I would have never heard of that word otherwise. I know how that nickname sounds, so I must assure you it's nothing dirty! He does fantastic interviews, mostly with musicians. It's all on Youtube and worth a watch.

So yeah, getting the SERVIETTES/SPANAKOPITA off the rip was cool to see and really helped fill this thing out. Got stuck on a few archaic words, a couple wrong squares didn't help either, but still very fun solve for a Saturday.

So much of a puzzle’s perceived difficulty depends on my mood and connection to the clues. Looking back, I have a gold star this week for Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, but used reveals on Wednesday and (somehow 🤗) Tuesday.

Personality, humor, fresh and zingy answers, deft cluing, paucity of junkness – hallmarks of Kameron’s puzzles.  They are not just fill-ins, they are rich experiences.  What a gift to have this sublime and talented artist / technician / entertainer cross our paths, and to have another opus today.

Fresh answers?  Today, a third of the answers – that’s right, one out of three – have appeared in the Times 80+ years of crosswords four times or less.  Wow!  

I love the brain that wasn’t satisfied to come up with a direct clue for LENS CAPS – what is almost always offered – but rather made that ordinary answer shine with [They’re taken off for boudoir photos].  

Or even just this: STENTS and “stent” have been clued more than 200 times in the major crossword outlets, but never using the misdirecting word “channel” as in today’s clue.  

Part of my fill-in was “Whee!”, and part was crunch, and all was rich, Kameron – as usual.  Thank you for your gift and for another splendid outing!
Crossing STEEVE with SERIESE felt a bit mean. Also, the clue for SLEEVELESST should have indicated that it’s an abbreviation.

(Apparently) unrelated coincidences like this freak me out:

“A PENG is a giant bird that transforms from a Kun, a giant fish, in Chinese mythology” according to Wikipedia. With oodles of caveats after that, but work with me here.

Yet apparently there is no linguistic relation between the large bird-fish we call ‘penguin’ and the Peng-kun? Someone please tell me I’m wrong.
Street team???

FWIW, found about the photo in today's Wordplay column: Wikipedia "Glen Lyon FPSO (2016): A colossal Floating Production, Storage, and Offloading vessel measuring 270 meters long. It operates west of Shetland in the UK sector of the North Sea at the Schiehallion and Loyal oil fields." "The Glen Lyon is a 100,000-tonne, 880-ft-long floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO). The ship was built in South Korea and is anchored to the seabed at the Schiehallion and Loyal oil fields in the North Sea in waters 1,300ft deep.[1][2] According to BP, it is the largest "harsh-water" FPSO ship in the world." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Lyon_(ship)

KAC Saturday?

I. Am. In.


( Good ol’ RIATA making a comeback, perchance? )

The Wordplay column gives us a hint about the root of the word "STEEVE" and also the word "stevedore."

[27A. [Load from the dock] solves to STEEVE here, which is an archaic English verb. The double E in this entry strikes me as odd whenever I see it because I think of STEEVE as an action taken by a stevedore, but that jaunty term is of Spanish etymology. Both go back to the Latin “stipare,” though, eventually.]

From my online search, "stipare" in Latin means to crowd, to press together, to compress, or to surround closely, to pack tightly or stuff, to throng around or escort (as a crowd around a leader).

That sounds like what a stevedore does. I can't think of any more words with this root, though.

Filled in the top half of this puzzle in decent time, but got hung up on the lower half, save for a few entries.  I "knew" the entry for BELLEAMIE but could not coax that out of my cranium until some crosses burst the dam.  Add in two typos and it forced a couple of look ups.  But a pretty good Saturday for me overall, nice puzzle.

This was fun, and more challenging than my time would suggest. (Half my average, close to my best.) It takes more than two to make a theme, right? REAREND + ARSES? TIL that ANTIRUST has the same number of letters as ANodized. I love ERICCARLE's work. In our house we have an Elephant and Piggy poster signed by Mo Willems that my wife got at the ERICCARLE Museum. Yes, we love Elephant and Piggy, too, and so do our granddaughters. I think I get why my comment was emu'ed yesterday, although I don't agree with it. Nevertheless, here's my favorite mondegreen from John Prine. https://youtu.be/Uvjvrsxsat8?si=fnEGxLq7q4McNMY7

Solved it unaided, but took over thirty minutes and I was a bit surprised when I heard the music. Quite few entries that I didn't know or about which I was not fully confident: ALFRE, STEEVE (went with this based on "stevedore"), SPANAKOPITA/DANSKO (the dish rang bells and "spanako" suggested "spinach"), BELLEAMIE (made approximate sense in translation), COMTE, PENG, STREETTEAM (never heard of this, but it made sense), BALLERS (as clued).

Quite a lot of "niche" stuff today, but perhaps only to me and I enjoyed (and met) the challenge.

Nice Saturday puzzle. Thanks!

"...you recognize Kameron Austin Collins as a sharp, witty constructor whose grids can pull a fearsome punch.”

I did, and seeing his name on a puzzle used to strike fear in me. Up until the last one that was published, when it turned out to be a walk in the park. So this time I was not as fearful, and it turned out to be with good reason.

This was a very nice puzzle. I knew Stevedore, so it was pretty easy to pull STEEVE out of that. SPANAKOPITA appeared like magic. I've owned DANSKO shoes. And SERVIETTES I knew from French and Spanish classes  (servilletas), though I had no idea that was the term used in Britain. RIATA was a gimme, as most long-time solvers know.

But I found little misdirection, too many straightforward answers, like MAGI and BREA, and the puzzle went by way too fast. I look forward to the end of the kinder, gentler KAC puzzles, especially on a Saturday.

Despite being “Naticked”  in several places was able to reason out the correct fill.  I guess that counts as a proper Saturday puzzle. Was chuffed to get the gold star after being totally flummoxed  most of the time. Not up to speed on KAC as puzzle maker, gonna have to check out his previous Saturdays. Apparently he’s in the Pantheon with Katie and Robyn

Beautiful grid.
Much too easy for a Saturday, IMHO.
I put in several guesses, thinking that they were probably wrong because they seemed too obvious for a Saturday.
They were all correct.

The allusion to "boudoir photos", however, gave a smile...and a blush.

Good morning! Sailed along pretty well until I got to the SW where I mucked about a bit, but it came together.
32D was thinking Its..... (easy? good?)
46D for some reason Egg came to mind.
Re: SW...am I the only one who ALWAYS pictures the grid of Manhattan to orient my N, S, E, W? 
45 years living away from NYC, but I'm still a NYer.
Disappointingly straightforward for a Saturday. I enjoy the usual 30-minute-or-so struggle, but was able to wrap tgis one up in 12.
41D might be my favorite of all time.

I feel I'm being gaslight at this point. A Saturday where I am able to put in many answers easily on first run through?  Quick trip to the archives says I am not the crazy one here.

Cling is not Saturday level. Bring back Saturday level.
Started out way too easy, but then somehow got harder. I knew PENG immediately, thanks to MST3K: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EiJylMyfu9I
Was thinking surely 35D can’t be the hardcore dance style GABBER, that’s too obscure even for a Saturday as clued. But you meant GABBER, someone who talks a lot and won’t shut up. Right . . .
spanaKopita – those wily Greeks and their K's instead of C's. Took me a good bit of flyspecking before the happy music played. Terrific fun puzzle with some grade A cluing.

Yessir, one HELLUVA puzzle, there, KAC....chock full of words I've never heard, will never use, and entered only unwillingly.  
BALLER
STEEVE
STREET TEAM
PENG
COMTE
GABBER
DANSKO

I would add that a "medium" is generally a fake claiming to forge communication between the living and the dead.  ESP is a real phenomenon...and not nearly the same thing.  

I did like seeing HYDROMETER (with DHubby the winemaker across the table from me.  Sigh...those days are behind us.)  
Aaaand we have a MINARET, but no muezzin.  
Just didn't find this  very interesting or lively....
Sorry, but "it don't mean a thing if you ain't got that swing!"
Bah! The northwest corner confuddled me. Good puzzle though.
Serviettes made me think of that goofy Manners the Butler, saving people from the terrible inconvenience of napkins that wouldn't stay on your lap. Yep, I'm that old.
How does French beauty resolve to belle amie? That means beautiful friend..
I had "lasso" before I had RIATA. I had never heard of RIATA but now I know how to make one: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/X9PaOtvf0c8

Would somebody please tell Sam Ezersky that RIATA is a perfectly reasonable Spelling Bee word? He keeps okaying the yogurt and cucumber sauce that is close to it, but ignoring this fine word. (Actually, I think we’ve all been telling him this for years.)

Relieved to see that at least a few others struggled with this one. For me? - just well above my pay grade. Completely stuck in more than a couple of places. No big deal. And... puzzle find. A Sunday from January 26, 2014 by Daniel A. Finan with the title: "It's all relative." Really unusual - all the theme answers were in pairs and the 'clue' was in part related to their positions in the puzzle. A couple of examples. 6-down "73-down relatively" NOWAYJOSE 73-down "See 6-down" MYDEADBODY (so the implication was 'over my dead body' 3-Down "See 51-down" ASPELL 51-down "3-down relatively" BEWITCHED (so the implication was 'under a spell')_ 12-Down "93-down relatively" TALKTOYOULATER 93-Down "See 12-down" ANDOUT (so the implication for that one was 'over and out') And there were more. Think about the other ones. Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=1/26/2014&h=6d ....
Fun one! I honestly thought I was on the archives until I came to the comments. Lots of tricky misdirects, and I can even forgive ETNA when it teaches me something new.
Fun crossword and although platform shoes weren't part of the puzzle, I went looking at how shoe fashions have changed over time. And Spanakopita would be delicious right now!
Just curious… If the clue is in Spanish (Comprende), shouldn’t the answer be in Spanish? That tripped me up!

And... off topic, but 21 letter answer that  somehow crept into my head this morning: 

INTHEEYEOFTHEBEHOLDER

And... nope. Never been in a puzzle. And even BEHOLDER has only been an answer 4 times. 

Sorry for the drift. 

....

I am so impressed by people who are able to solve Friday and Saturday puzzles unaided. I hope to get there someday. In the meantime, I will continue to solve easy mode on Fridays and use autocorrect on Saturday puzzles.

What's it all about, ALFrE?  I was so sure that the actress was ALFIE Woodard that I didn't change the I to an R -- not even when I had STIEETTEAM at 4D.

Don't ask.

I didn't know the shoe.  Having LEN?CAPS at "they're taken off for boudoir photos", I had no idea.  But Jay LENO is on late at night when you're in the boudoir and LENO is funny, so I guessed his CAPS would be funny too -- and totally inappropriate for a boudoir photo.  So I wrote in LENO CAPS-- though not with great confidence.  DANOKO seemed as good a name for a shoe as any other.

Don't ask.

After running the alphabet for BA?LERS for the ostentatious spenders, I decided not to write anything in at all.  Should have picked the L for something that was at least a real word, though I never heard BALLERS used that way?

Don't ask.

An ostentatious belly flop for me today.  A huge amount of dumbness displayed.  Happily I didn't miss out on the cash prize for solving this thing because there isn't one.
Finally, what the people have been asking for: a puzzle with apparent typos for answers, with OO LA LA and SLEEVELESS T
Confused by how SWEETY is ‘in one spelling’ (11D). Isn’t that the only spelling?
Yeah, this one wasn't my favorite. Just didn't mesh with the clues, and some were just odd. 4/10
Why is it that when I solve a puzzle in about my average time it feels like I was barely able to finish it?

Wow, that was like pulling teeth. I do feel I was clue-bullied. (see constructor's note.) Case in point: Gruyere de COMTE is sometimes marketed as simply COMTE, for reasons I am unable to discern. I've never heard of it either way, and I do like fancy cheese. GABBER was just annoying. I was thinking of that one fraternity brother who always got sloppy drunk and tried to kiss random girls.BALLERS was also annoying, as clued. But SPANAKOPITA just about made up for it.

51A.  Chinese bird from a fish called Kun?
Sorry, I could then only think about A Fish Called Wanda, not any Chinese mythology. 

Good KAC puzzle, thanks.
Alfre Woodard has had so many wonderful roles, but Trekkies might remember her for her great role as Zefram Cochrane’s assistant in “Star Trek: First Contact”.

Rare Saturday puzzle perfectly synched to my brain! PB time, the answers flowed like water, barely a misstep along the way! A real pleasure when everything clicks into place. BALLERS, DAP and STEEVE were the last pieces to fall, and they didn’t put up much of a fight.
Whew, if Mr Collins eased up on this one, I need to get in better shape before he resumes his bullying ways! This was a fun workout.
HELLUVA puzzle but that's too be expected from KAC
No word checks today! Guess it must be rated easy but I really enjoyed it. Had to trust that it would eventually fill in. Had hurl for TOSS for a while and thought it might be Yeet.
After slogging through this one on autocheck, I decided to cheer myself up by scheduling a root canal. That was rough. Mimosa time!
Kudos on finding a photo of someone about to STEEVE while wearing DANSKOs and a SLEEVELESST.
Could someone explain lens cap? Don't hou have to remove it for all photos?
Thanks, Wikipedia!
Can someone help me maintain my sanity and explain why OOLALA made it versus OOHLALA? Barry, MOL, anyone? Bueler?
I guess I will need a STENT in my heart channel. Please.
Enjoyable puzzle but done in by the K in dansko.  Annoying.

Oo-la-la, a bilingual puzzle! I must say, en passant, that I feared for my streak. I thought about asking my belle amie for a little help, but she told me that would not be solving it à la loyale and I must do it tout seul. Sacré bleu!

Unfamiliar with the term, we searched "steeve" and the first result was Minecraft Steve. Then we searched "steeve boat" and got Minecraft Steve in a boat. Not sure whether this is an issue isolated to the phones of those 30 and under but it did seem to suggest the word is slightly obscure.

I'll be honest, when I see KAC is the constructor for a puzzle, I groan. His grids are always full of misdirects which I find more irritating than playful. I appreciate learning a new thing or two in a grid, especially on the later days of the week, and I can enjoy a few wordplay tricks, but I find that KAC usually oversaturates for my taste.

However, I did remember that the last KAC grid was enjoyable, so I had high hopes for this one. But I think this is the worst of both worlds. Fans of the difficulty which I find obnoxious won't be pleased, as this was (mostly) straightforward, but there were still traces of this via some gnarly words. STEEVE is a word that could be a fun archaic word to learn, except that it's crossed with SERVIETTES and SERIESE, so it's just a meat grinder. RIATA is crossing some of the same downs as well, in case it wasn't tough enough. 

So there's not enough misdirection to please the hardcore challenge KAC fans, but there are enough difficult words to annoy people like me. I'm not at all looking forward to KAC returning to his trademark difficulty, but at least it should mean that his fans can get enjoyment out of it. This grid, to me, seems like a whiff on all fronts.

A blouse is a blouse because it's blousy.  That means it's not form-fitting and billows away from the body.  This may be out of necessity for women's clothing before stretch fabric, so that women of various bosom sizes could all wear the same size blouse, which is why we say some people "fill out" their clothing.  But it's only fashion that dictates that blouses are only for women; one need only think of the swashbuckling pirates in the movies and realize that they often wear the same type of garment.

Also, a tank top and a sleeveless tee differ in that a sleeveless tee is just a regular T-shirt without any sleeve at all, like the one in the column picture (although I really think that's a regular tee with the sleeves rolled up). I learned to make spanakopita from years of cooking holiday dinners with my half-Greek sister-in-law. Using store bought frozen phyllo simplifies the process and gives excellent results. We prefer spanakopita triangles so it takes longer than making a single dish, but it's worth it for the higher phyllo to filling ratio.  Cut the phyllo into long strips, brush each strip with butter to get a crispy, crunchy result, add a generous spoonful of spinach mixture, and fold.
